claim: DPP9 removes dipeptides from N-termini of substrates having a proline or alanine in second position.
source: The aminopeptidase DPP9 removes dipeptides from N-termini of substrates having a proline or alanine in second position.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by citations to Yu et al., 2010 and Waumans et al., 2015 in the introduction.

claim: DPP9 interacts with Filamin A.
source: We identified a novel interaction of DPP9 with Filamin A, which recruits DPP9 to Syk, a central kinase in B-cell signalling.
evidence: Supported by yeast two-hybrid screening, pull-down assays, co-immunoprecipitation, and proximity ligation assays shown in Figure 1.

claim: DPP9 cleaves Syk to produce a neo N-terminus with serine in position 1.
source: We show that DPP9 cleaves Syk to produce a neo N-terminus with serine in position 1.
evidence: Supported by in vitro cleavage assays and mass spectrometry analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Ser1 strongly influences Syk stability.
source: Pulse-chases combined with mutagenesis studies reveal that Ser1 strongly influences Syk stability.
evidence: Supported by cycloheximide chase experiments with Syk mutants shown in Figure 5E-H.

claim: DPP9 silencing reduces Cbl interaction with Syk.
source: Furthermore, DPP9 silencing reduces Cbl interaction with Syk, suggesting that DPP9 processing is a prerequisite for Syk ubiquitination.
evidence: Supported by proximity ligation assays shown in Figure 5I and J.

claim: DPP9 inhibition stabilizes Syk.
source: Consistently, DPP9 inhibition stabilizes Syk, thereby modulating Syk signalling.
evidence: Supported by cycloheximide chase experiments with DPP9 inhibitor 1G244 shown in Figure 6F and G.

claim: DPP9 is a negative regulator of Syk.
source: Taken together, we demonstrate DPP9 as a negative regulator of Syk and conclude that DPP9 is a novel integral aminopeptidase of the N-end rule pathway.
evidence: Supported by multiple experiments showing DPP9 cleaves Syk leading to its degradation and modulation of signaling.

claim: DPP9 is a novel integral aminopeptidase of the N-end rule pathway.
source: Taken together, we demonstrate DPP9 as a negative regulator of Syk and conclude that DPP9 is a novel integral aminopeptidase of the N-end rule pathway.
evidence: Inferred from data showing DPP9 cleavage exposes N-terminal serine that affects protein stability.

claim: DPP8 and DPP9 are the only known intracellular members of the DPPIV family.
source: DPP8 and DPP9 are the only known intracellular members of this family, sharing 60% homology with a higher conservation (>90% identity) in their active site (Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2013.

claim: DPP9, but not DPP8, is rate-limiting for the hydrolysis of proline-containing peptides in the cytoplasm.
source: However, DPP9, but not DPP8, is rate-limiting for the hydrolysis of proline-containing peptides in the cytoplasm, and plays a role in maturation of antigenic peptides for presentation on MHC class I alleles (Geiss-Friedlander et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Geiss-Friedlander et al., 2009.

claim: Knock-in mice expressing an inactive variant of DPP9 die 8–24 hr after birth.
source: Knock-in mice expressing an inactive variant of DPP9 die 8–24 hr after birth, demonstrating its importance for neonatal survival which is not compensated by DPP8 (Gall et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gall et al., 2013.

claim: DPP9 shows a broad tissue distribution.
source: DPP9 shows a broad tissue distribution (Qi et al., 2003; Ajami et al., 2004), localizes to the cytosol (Ajami et al., 2004), nucleus (Justa-Schuch et al., 2014), and to the leading edge of migrating cells (Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Qi et al., 2003 and Ajami et al., 2004.

claim: DPP9 localizes to the cytosol.
source: DPP9 shows a broad tissue distribution (Qi et al., 2003; Ajami et al., 2004), localizes to the cytosol (Ajami et al., 2004), nucleus (Justa-Schuch et al., 2014), and to the leading edge of migrating cells (Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ajami et al., 2004.

claim: DPP9 localizes to the nucleus.
source: DPP9 shows a broad tissue distribution (Qi et al., 2003; Ajami et al., 2004), localizes to the cytosol (Ajami et al., 2004), nucleus (Justa-Schuch et al., 2014), and to the leading edge of migrating cells (Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Justa-Schuch et al., 2014.

claim: DPP9 localizes to the leading edge of migrating cells.
source: DPP9 shows a broad tissue distribution (Qi et al., 2003; Ajami et al., 2004), localizes to the cytosol (Ajami et al., 2004), nucleus (Justa-Schuch et al., 2014), and to the leading edge of migrating cells (Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2015.

claim: DPP9 is linked to Akt signalling.
source: DPP9 is linked to several pathways including Akt signalling (Yao et al., 2011; Pilla et al., 2013), activation of pro-inflammatory M1 macrophages (Matheeussen et al., 2013), cell migration (Zhang et al., 2015) and apoptosis of specific cell lines (Matheeussen et al., 2013; Spagnuolo et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Yao et al., 2011 and Pilla et al., 2013.

claim: DPP9 is linked to activation of pro-inflammatory M1 macrophages.
source: DPP9 is linked to several pathways including Akt signalling (Yao et al., 2011; Pilla et al., 2013), activation of pro-inflammatory M1 macrophages (Matheeussen et al., 2013), cell migration (Zhang et al., 2015) and apoptosis of specific cell lines (Matheeussen et al., 2013; Spagnuolo et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Matheeussen et al., 2013.

claim: DPP9 is linked to cell migration.
source: DPP9 is linked to several pathways including Akt signalling (Yao et al., 2011; Pilla et al., 2013), activation of pro-inflammatory M1 macrophages (Matheeussen et al., 2013), cell migration (Zhang et al., 2015) and apoptosis of specific cell lines (Matheeussen et al., 2013; Spagnuolo et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2015.

claim: DPP9 is linked to apoptosis of specific cell lines.
source: DPP9 is linked to several pathways including Akt signalling (Yao et al., 2011; Pilla et al., 2013), activation of pro-inflammatory M1 macrophages (Matheeussen et al., 2013), cell migration (Zhang et al., 2015) and apoptosis of specific cell lines (Matheeussen et al., 2013; Spagnuolo et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Matheeussen et al., 2013 and Spagnuolo et al., 2013.

claim: SUMO1 was identified as a novel DPP9 associating protein.
source: Previously, we identified SUMO1 as a novel DPP9 associating protein, and demonstrated that SUMO1 acts as an allosteric activator of DPP9 (Pilla et al., 2013, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pilla et al., 2013 and 2012.

claim: SUMO1 acts as an allosteric activator of DPP9.
source: Previously, we identified SUMO1 as a novel DPP9 associating protein, and demonstrated that SUMO1 acts as an allosteric activator of DPP9 (Pilla et al., 2013, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pilla et al., 2013 and 2012.

claim: Filamin A (FLNA) was identified as a novel interacting partner of DPP9 in a yeast two-hybrid assay.
source: Now we report filamin A (FLNA) as a novel interacting partner of DPP9, which we identified in a yeast two-hybrid assay.
evidence: Supported by yeast two-hybrid screening described in the methods.

claim: FLNA is an actin binding protein that cross-links actin filaments into orthogonal networks.
source: FLNA is an actin binding protein that cross-links actin filaments into orthogonal networks, and is important for cell stiffening, cell adhesion and cell migration (Nakamura et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nakamura et al., 2011.

claim: FLNA is important for cell stiffening, cell adhesion and cell migration.
source: FLNA is an actin binding protein that cross-links actin filaments into orthogonal networks, and is important for cell stiffening, cell adhesion and cell migration (Nakamura et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nakamura et al., 2011.

claim: The interaction between DPP9 and FLNA was mapped to FLNA repeats 5–7.
source: Surprisingly, we mapped the interaction between DPP9 and FLNA to repeats 5–7.
evidence: Supported by yeast two-hybrid assay and pull-down assays shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: Syk is known to bind to FLNA repeat 5.
source: Apart from DPP9, so far only the non-receptor tyrosine kinase Syk is known to bind to FLNA repeat 5 (Falet et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Falet et al., 2010.

claim: Recombinant DPP9 binds directly to recombinant FLAG tagged FLNA.
source: Pull-down assays showing direct interaction between recombinant DPP9 and recombinant FLAG tagged wt FLNA or a mutated form of FLAG-FLNA (lacking repeats 4, 9, 12, 17, 19, 21, and 23).
evidence: Supported by pull-down assay shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Recombinant DPP9 binds directly to GST-FLNA construct containing repeats 5–7 but not to GST-FLNA construct containing repeats 6–7.
source: Recombinant DPP9 binds directly to GST- FLNA construct containing repeats 5–7 but not to GST-FLNA construct containing repeats 6–7.
evidence: Supported by pull-down assay shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Endogenous FLNA co-immunoprecipitates with endogenous DPP9 from HeLa cells in the presence of the sulfhydryl cross-linker DPDPB.
source: Co-immunoprecipitation of endogenous FLNA with endogenous DPP9 from HeLa cells treated with different cross-linkers. Binding was observed in the presence of the sulfhydryl cross-linker DPDPB.
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation assay shown in Figure 1D.

claim: DPP8 does not bind to DPP9 in the presence of DPDPB.
source: To control for the specificity of the cross link, we blotted for DPP8, which did not bind to DPP9 in the presence of DPDPB
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation control shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The number of DPP9-FLNA PLA signals per cell is significantly decreased in cells silenced for FLNA compared to cells treated with NT siRNA.
source: The number of PLA signals is significantly decreased in cells silenced for FLNA compared to cells treated with NT siRNA.
evidence: Supported by proximity ligation assay shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: The amino terminus of Syk contains a DPP9 consensus cleavage site with an alanine in second position (Met-Ala).
source: Interestingly, the amino terminus of Syk contains a DPP9 consensus cleavage site Xaa-Pro/Ala (Connolly et al., 2008; Ajami et al., 2004) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and B) with an alanine in second position (Met-Ala), suggesting that Syk may be a DPP9 substrate.
evidence: Supported by sequence analysis and citations to Connolly et al., 2008 and Ajami et al., 2004.

claim: DPP9 binds to the Syk (1–31) peptide with a KD of 52 ± 4 µM.
source: We observed direct binding of DPP9 to the Syk (1–31) peptide with a KD of 52 ± 4 µM (Figure 2C and E), suggesting a dynamic and transient interaction.
evidence: Supported by Surface Plasmon Resonance assays shown in Figure 2C and E.

claim: The inactive DPP9 variant S730G shows more than a five-fold reduction in its affinity to the Syk (1–31) peptide (KD of 284 ± 27 µM) compared to wild type DPP9.
source: Furthermore, an inactive DPP9 variant in which the serine in the active site was mutated to a glycine residue (DPP9 S730G) showed more than a five-fold reduction in its affinity to the Syk (1–31) peptide (KD of 284 ± 27 µM) compared to the wild type protein (Figure 2C and E).
evidence: Supported by Surface Plasmon Resonance assays shown in Figure 2C and E.

claim: Wild type DPP9 binds to Syk△MA (3–31) peptide with a lower affinity (KD of 156 ± 60 µM) compared to Syk (1-31) peptide.
source: A lower affinity (KD of 156 ± 60 µM) was also observed between wild type DPP9 and a Syk△MA (3–31) peptide, which lacks the first two amino acids Met-Ala (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: Supported by Surface Plasmon Resonance assays shown in Figure 2D and E.

claim: After six hours incubation, DPP9 cleaved more than 99% of the Syk (1-31) peptide to remove the first two residues.
source: Mass spectrometry analysis of these reactions revealed that after six hours incubation, DPP9 had cleaved more than 99% of this peptide to remove the first two residues (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by in vitro cleavage assay and mass spectrometry shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Processing of Syk (1-31) peptide by DPP9 was strongly reduced to only 6.2% in control samples treated with the allosteric DPP8/9 peptide inhibitor SLRFLYEG.
source: Processing was strongly reduced to only 6.2% in control samples treated with the allosteric DPP8/9 peptide inhibitor SLRFLYEG (Pilla et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by in vitro cleavage assay shown in Figure 3A.

claim: No cleavage of Syk (1-31) peptide was observed in the presence of the inactive variant DPP9 S730G.
source: No cleavage was observed in the presence of the inactive variant DPP9 S730G (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by in vitro cleavage assay shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Exposure of HeLa cells to SLRFLYEG resulted in a significant reduction in PLA signals corresponding to DPP9-Syk interaction events.
source: Consistently, exposure of cells to SLRFLYEG resulted in a significant reduction in PLA signals corresponding to DPP9-Syk interaction events, compared to the control cells treated with the carrier peptide only (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: Supported by proximity ligation assay shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: Treatment of cells with the competitive DPP9 inhibitor 1G244 led to a clear decrease in the number of Syk-DPP9 PLA signals.
source: Likewise, treatment of cells with the competitive DPP9 inhibitor 1G244 (Wu et al., 2009) also led to a clear decrease in the number of Syk-DPP9 PLA signals (Figures 3D and E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by proximity ligation assay shown in Figures 3D and E.

claim: The association of DPP9 with FLNA was not significantly altered by 1G244 treatment.
source: For control, we measured the association of DPP9 with FLNA, which was not significantly altered by the 1G244 treatment (Figure 3F and G).
evidence: Supported by proximity ligation assay shown in Figure 3F and G.

claim: The cellular localization of DPP9 is altered in FLNA silenced cells.
source: Strikingly, immunofluorescence microscopy images show a drastic change in the cellular localization of DPP9 in FLNA silenced cells compared to control cells treated with non-targeting siRNA (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Upon FLNA silencing, DPP9 was no longer observed at the plasma membrane and was detected less in the cytosol, showing elevated levels in the nucleus.
source: In particular, upon FLNA silencing, DPP9 was no longer observed at the plasma membrane and was detected less in the cytosol, showing elevated levels in the nucleus (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: A significant reduction in the number of DPP9-Syk interaction events was detected in FLNA silenced cells compared to cells treated with non-targeting siRNA.
source: We detected a significant reduction in the number of DPP9-Syk interaction events in the FLNA silenced cells as indicated by a lower number of PLA dots (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: Supported by proximity ligation assay shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: The DPP9-kd cell line shows a 40% reduction in its capacity to cleave the artificial substrate Gly-Pro-AMC (GP-AMC).
source: This cell line shows a 40% reduction in its capacity to cleave the artificial substrate Gly-Pro-AMC (GP-AMC), which can be cleaved by DPP8, DPP9 and DPPIV.
evidence: Supported by activity assay shown in Figure 5A.

claim: At least a 50% reduction in DPP9 protein levels was detected in DPP9-kd cells compared to the control parental cell line.
source: Additionally, we detected at least a 50% reduction in DPP9 protein levels in these cells compared to the control parental cell line (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: Supported by Western blot shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Higher Syk protein levels were observed in the DPP9-kd cell line compared to wild type cells when transfected with equal amounts of plasmid DNA encoding Syk-FLAG.
source: Surprisingly, although we transfected wild type and DPP9-kd cells with equal amounts of plasmid DNA encoding C-terminal FLAG tagged Syk (Syk-FLAG), higher Syk protein levels were observed in the DPP9-kd cell line (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by Western blot shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Syk-FLAG is degraded in HeLa cells with a half-life of 6 hr.
source: We found that Syk-FLAG is degraded in HeLa cells with a half-life of 6 hr.
evidence: Supported by cycloheximide chase experiments shown in Figures 5C and D.

claim: Syk-FLAG was more stable in the DPP9-kd cells compared to the control parental HeLa cells.
source: Remarkably, Syk-FLAG was more stable in the DPP9-kd cells compared to the control parental HeLa cells (Figures 5C and D).
evidence: Supported by cycloheximide chase experiments shown in Figures 5C and D.

claim: The single mutation of Ser 3 to a Gly or a Val clearly increased the half-life of the SykS3G and SykS3V variants compared to wild-type Syk.
source: Strikingly, the single mutation of Ser 3 to a Gly or a Val clearly increased the half-life of the SykS3G and SykS3V variants (Figure 5E and F), compared to the wild-type protein.
evidence: Supported by cycloheximide chase experiments shown in Figure 5E and F.

claim: An increased half-life of Syk was measured for the SykA2D variant, which cannot be processed by DPP9.
source: Furthermore, an increased half-life of Syk was also measured for the SykA2D variant, which cannot be processed by DPP9 (Figure 5G and H).
evidence: Supported by cycloheximide chase experiments shown in Figure 5G and H.

claim: Syk is negatively regulated by the E3 ubiquitin ligase Cbl.
source: Syk is negatively regulated by the E3 ubiquitin ligase Cbl (Ota et al., 2000; Paolini et al., 2001; Joazeiro et al., 1999; Rao et al., 2001a; Sohn et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ota et al., 2000; Paolini et al., 2001; Joazeiro et al., 1999; Rao et al., 2001a; Sohn et al., 2003.

claim: Proteasome inhibition in natural killer cells results in the accumulation of ubiquitinated Syk species.
source: Proteasome inhibition in natural killer cells results in the accumulation of ubiquitinated Syk species, suggesting that ubiquitination targets the kinase for proteasomal degradation (Paolini et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Paolini et al., 2001.

claim: An interaction between endogenous Cbl and Syk was established in HeLa cells by PLA.
source: Performing PLAs we established an interaction between endogenous Cbl and Syk in HeLa cells (Figure 5I).
evidence: Supported by proximity ligation assay shown in Figure 5I.

claim: The number of PLA signals corresponding to a Syk-Cbl interaction were significantly lower in the DPP9-kd cells compared to the control parental HeLa cells.
source: Strikingly, the number of PLA signals corresponding to a Syk-Cbl interaction were significantly lower in the DPP9-kd cells compared to the control parental HeLa cells (Figure 5I and J), suggesting a functional cross-talk between DPP9 and Cbl.
evidence: Supported by proximity ligation assay shown in Figure 5I and J.

claim: DPP9 is expressed in DG-75 B cells.
source: Western blot analysis, activity assays and indirect immunofluorescence verify the expression of DPP9 in these cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by Western blot, activity assays and immunofluorescence shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The binding of FLNA to Syk and DPP9 is conserved in DG-75 cells.
source: Next, PLA analysis shows that the binding of FLNA to Syk and DPP9 is conserved in DG-75 cells (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: Supported by proximity ligation assay shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: Clear PLA signals corresponding to an interaction between DPP9 and Syk were observed in DG-75 cells.
source: Importantly, clear PLA signals corresponding to an interaction between DPP9 and Syk were also observed in these cells (Figure 6C and D and Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by proximity ligation assay shown in Figure 6C and D and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: DPP8 did not appear to interact with Syk in DG-75 cells, although it is expressed in these cells.
source: Of note, DPP8, which shares 60% homology to DPP9, did not appear to interact with Syk, although it is expressed in these cells.
evidence: Supported by proximity ligation assay shown in Figure 6C and D.

claim: No interaction above background level was observed between Syk and the membrane protease DPPIV.
source: Similarly, no interaction above back-ground level was observed between Syk and the membrane protease DPPIV, which shares 26% homology with DPP9 (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: Supported by proximity ligation assay shown in Figure 6C and D.

claim: Syk was stable in unstimulated DG-75 B cells over a time period of 6 hr.
source: Whereas Syk was stable in unstimulated B cells over a time period of 6 hr, upon stimulation of the BCR, Syk was degraded with a half-life of 2 hr (+ stimulation, Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by cycloheximide chase experiments shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Upon stimulation of the BCR, Syk was degraded with a half-life of 2 hr in DG-75 cells.
source: Whereas Syk was stable in unstimulated B cells over a time period of 6 hr, upon stimulation of the BCR, Syk was degraded with a half-life of 2 hr (+ stimulation, Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by cycloheximide chase experiments shown in Figure 6E.

claim: A clear stabilization of Syk was observed in stimulated DG-75 cells which were treated with the proteasome inhibitor MG132.
source: As expected, a clear stabilization of Syk was observed in stimulated DG-75 cells which were treated with the proteasome inhibitor MG132 (Figure 6F and G).
evidence: Supported by cycloheximide chase experiments shown in Figure 6F and G.

claim: Treatment of stimulated DG-75 cells with the DPP8/9 inhibitor 1G244 resulted in a clear stabilization of Syk.
source: Notably, consistent with our findings showing stabilization of Syk in DPP9-kd HeLa cells, treatment of stimulated DG-75 cells with the DPP8/9 inhibitor 1G244 resulted in a clear stabilization of Syk (Figure 6F and G).
evidence: Supported by cycloheximide chase experiments shown in Figure 6F and G.

claim: Clear signals corresponding to the phosphorylation of Syk on Y323 were observed upon stimulation of DG-75 cells.
source: CHX chase experiments on BCR stimulated cells show clear signals corresponding to the phosphorylation of Syk on Y323 upon stimulation of DG-75 cells (Figure 6H and I), which clearly dropped in intensity over time.
evidence: Supported by cycloheximide chase experiments shown in Figure 6H and I.

claim: The intensities of signals corresponding to Syk pY323 did not drop as rapidly in 1G244 treated cells compared to control cells.
source: Notably, the intensities of signals corresponding to Syk pY323 did not drop as rapidly in 1G244 treated cells.
evidence: Supported by cycloheximide chase experiments shown in Figure 6H and I.

claim: Inhibition of DPP9 in stimulated B-cells resulted in a prolonged phosphorylation of Syk on Y352.
source: Remarkably, inhibition of DPP9 in stimulated B-cells resulted also in a prolonged phosphorylation of Syk on Y352 (Figure 7A and B), which is important both for the catalytic activity of Syk and for the activation of the proximal target Phospholipase C-γ2 (PLCγ2) (Tsang et al., 2008; Law et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by Western blot shown in Figure 7A and B.

claim: Syk Y352 is important both for the catalytic activity of Syk and for the activation of the proximal target Phospholipase C-γ2 (PLCγ2).
source: Remarkably, inhibition of DPP9 in stimulated B-cells resulted also in a prolonged phosphorylation of Syk on Y352 (Figure 7A and B), which is important both for the catalytic activity of Syk and for the activation of the proximal target Phospholipase C-γ2 (PLCγ2) (Tsang et al., 2008; Law et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to Tsang et al., 2008 and Law et al., 1996.

claim: Application of 1G244 to DG-75 cells triggered a rapid increase in Ca2+ fluxes, which occurred before the stimulation of the BCR.
source: Remarkably, application of 1G244 to DG-75 cells triggered a rapid increase in Ca2+ fluxes, which occurred before the stimulation of the BCR (Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by Ca2+ measurements shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Similar results of increased Ca2+ fluxes upon 1G244 treatment were observed in Ramos cells.
source: Similar results were also observed in Ramos cells, a second Burkitt's lymphoma cell line (Figure 7D).
evidence: Supported by Ca2+ measurements shown in Figure 7D.

claim: In the absence of BCR stimulation, the steady state levels of Syk were comparable in cells treated with 1G244 and in mock treated cells.
source: Furthermore, in the absence of BCR stimulation, the steady state levels of Syk were comparable in cells treated with 1G244 and in mock treated cells (no 1G244) (Figure 7E).
evidence: Supported by Western blot shown in Figure 7E.

claim: The phosphorylation levels of Syk (Syk-pY352) and PLCγ2 (PLCγ2-pY753) were higher in the 1G244 treated cells in the absence of BCR stimulation.
source: However, as we tested for the levels of active syk and PLCγ2, we found that the phosphorylation levels of Syk (Syk-pY352) and PLCγ2 (PLCγ2-pY753) were higher in the 1G244 treated cells (Figure 7E).
evidence: Supported by Western blot shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Immunoprecipitation assays of DG-75 cell lysates with antibodies against phospho-tyrosine revealed higher levels of phosphorylated Syk and PLCγ2 upon DPP9 inhibition with 1G244, independently of BCR stimulation.
source: Immunoprecipitation assays of DG-75 cell lysates with antibodies against phospho-tyrosine (p-Y) (Figure 7F) also revealed higher levels of phosphorylated Syk and PLCγ2 upon DPP9 inhibition with 1G244 (Figure 7F), independently of BCR stimulation.
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation assay shown in Figure 7F.

claim: An increase in the steady state phosphorylation levels of PLCγ2 on pY753 was observed in DG75 cells treated with the allosteric inhibitor of DPP9 SLRFLYEG in the absence of BCR engagement.
source: Consistently, an increase in the steady state phosphorylation levels of PLCγ2 on pY753 was also observed in DG75 cells treated with the allosteric inhibitor of DPP9 SLRFLYEG in the absence of BCR engagement (Figure 7F).
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation assay shown in Figure 7F.

claim: BCR engagement under DPP9 inhibition revealed a more transient ERK1/2 phosphorylation profile compared to control cells.
source: While BCR engagement under DPP9 inhibition revealed a more transient ERK1/2 phosphorylation profile compared to control cells, it is important to note that the levels of ERK1/2 phosphorylation in resting cells were slightly augmented in cells that were treated with 1G244 (Figure 7 G and H).
evidence: Supported by Western blot shown in Figure 7G and H.

claim: The levels of ERK1/2 phosphorylation in resting cells were slightly augmented in cells that were treated with 1G244.
source: While BCR engagement under DPP9 inhibition revealed a more transient ERK1/2 phosphorylation profile compared to control cells, it is important to note that the levels of ERK1/2 phosphorylation in resting cells were slightly augmented in cells that were treated with 1G244 (Figure 7 G and H).
evidence: Supported by Western blot shown in Figure 7G and H.

claim: DPP9 inhibition in unstimulated cells stabilizes an active phosphorylated form of Syk, resulting in 'signal leakage' as measured by higher levels of phosphorylated PLCγ2 forms and increased Ca2+ fluxes.
source: These results are in line with the finding that DPP9 inhibition in unstimulated cells stabilizes an active phosphorylated form of Syk, resulting in 'signal leakage' as measured by higher levels of phosphorylated PLCγ2 forms and increased Ca2+ fluxes leading to reduced sensitivity to BCR engagement.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental results showing increased phosphorylation and Ca2+ fluxes upon DPP9 inhibition.

claim: DPP9 is an integral negative regulator of Syk signalling by terminating Syk activity through processing the amino terminus of the kinase.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that DPP9 is an integral negative regulator of Syk signalling by terminating Syk activity through processing the amino terminus of the kinase.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental results showing DPP9 cleaves Syk leading to its degradation and modulation of signaling.

claim: Syk is a central component of the B cell signalling.
source: Here, we report the identification of Syk as a novel endogenous substrate of DPP9. Being a central component of the B cell signalling, Syk initiates the phosphorylation of a cascade of downstream components, ultimately modulating cellular metabolism, cell migration, cell proliferation, apoptosis and gene transcription events (Mócsai et al., 2010; Lowell, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mócsai et al., 2010 and Lowell, 2011.

claim: Syk initiates the phosphorylation of a cascade of downstream components, ultimately modulating cellular metabolism, cell migration, cell proliferation, apoptosis and gene transcription events.
source: Being a central component of the B cell signalling, Syk initiates the phosphorylation of a cascade of downstream components, ultimately modulating cellular metabolism, cell migration, cell proliferation, apoptosis and gene transcription events (Mócsai et al., 2010; Lowell, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mócsai et al., 2010 and Lowell, 2011.

claim: Syk is activated following BCR engagement.
source: Syk is activated following BCR engagement, and is negatively regulated by phosphatases such as Shp-1 and PTPROt (Dustin et al., 1999; Alsadeq et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2006), and by the E3 ubiquitin ligase Cbl (Paolini et al., 2001; Joazeiro et al., 1999; Rao et al., 2001a; Sohn et al., 2003; Lupher et al., 1998; Ota and Samelson, 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple papers.

claim: Syk is negatively regulated by phosphatases such as Shp-1 and PTPROt.
source: Syk is activated following BCR engagement, and is negatively regulated by phosphatases such as Shp-1 and PTPROt (Dustin et al., 1999; Alsadeq et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2006), and by the E3 ubiquitin ligase Cbl (Paolini et al., 2001; Joazeiro et al., 1999; Rao et al., 2001a; Sohn et al., 2003; Lupher et al., 1998; Ota and Samelson, 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dustin et al., 1999; Alsadeq et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2006.

claim: DPP9 inhibition results in increased half-life of Syk and higher levels of active phosphorylated Syk pY352.
source: DPP9 inhibition results in increased half-life of Syk and higher levels of active phosphorylated Syk pY352, suggesting that DPP9 targets the active form of Syk for degradation.
evidence: Supported by cycloheximide chase experiments and Western blots shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: DPP9 targets the active form of Syk for degradation.
source: DPP9 inhibition results in increased half-life of Syk and higher levels of active phosphorylated Syk pY352, suggesting that DPP9 targets the active form of Syk for degradation.
evidence: Inferred from data showing DPP9 inhibition leads to accumulation of phosphorylated Syk.

claim: Y323 is a critical residue for interaction between Syk and Cbl.
source: Furthermore DPP9 inhibition results in a prolonged accumulation of Syk phosphorylated on Y323, which is a critical residue for interaction with Cbl (Yankee et al., 1999; Lupher et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to Yankee et al., 1999 and Lupher et al., 1998.

claim: Cleavage of Syk by DPP9 is an upstream event to Syk ubiquitination by Cbl.
source: Taken together, these results strongly suggest a cross talk between DPP9 and Cbl, in which cleavage of Syk by DPP9 is an up stream event to Syk ubiquitination by Cbl.
evidence: Inferred from data showing DPP9 silencing reduces Cbl-Syk interaction and DPP9 inhibition prolongs Syk pY323 accumulation.

claim: B cells possess 'tonic' signalling, which maintains a constitutive baseline signal in B cells.
source: In addition to activated BCR signalling, which relays on the binding of antigens to the BCR, B cells also possess the so-called 'tonic' signalling, which maintains a constitutive baseline signal in B cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Tonic signalling occurs in the absence of antigen binding, but is dependent on the presence and activity of the BCR and some BCR components such as Syk, PLCγ2 and ERK1/2.
source: Tonic signalling occurs in the absence of antigen binding, but nonetheless is dependent on the presence and activity of the BCR and some BCR components such as Syk, PLCγ2 and ERK1/2 (Monroe, 2006; Wienands et al., 1996; Shaffer and Schlissel, 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to Monroe, 2006; Wienands et al., 1996; Shaffer and Schlissel, 1997.

claim: Tonic signalling is essential for survival of B cells, including Burkitt lymphomas.
source: The molecular details regarding this pathway are only emerging but it is clear that tonic signalling is essential for survival of B cells, including Burkitt lymphomas (Corso et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Corso et al., 2016.

claim: By targeting Syk pY352 for degradation, DPP9 maintains low levels of activated Syk sufficient for tonic signalling.
source: We suggest that by targeting Syk pY352 for degradation, DPP9 maintains low levels of activated Syk sufficient for tonic signalling, and thus can influence the strength of the BCR signalling in response to antigen engagement.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on experimental data.

claim: By targeting Syk for degradation after BCR engagement, DPP9 can influence the duration of the response to antigen BCR binding.
source: By targeting Syk for degradation after BCR engagement, DPP9 can also influence the duration of the response to antigen BCR binding (Figure 8A and B).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on experimental data shown in Figure 8.

claim: MetAPs are considered an integral part of the N-end rule pathway.
source: Nonetheless, MetAPs are considered an integral part of the N-end rule pathway, because these residues may be converted to Ac/N-degrons (Hwang et al., 2010b), albeit to different efficiencies.
evidence: Supported by citation to Hwang et al., 2010b.

claim: DPP9 is a second integral aminopeptidase of the N-end rule pathway.
source: Our data place DPP9 as a second integral aminopeptidase of the N-end rule pathway.
evidence: Inferred from data showing DPP9 cleavage exposes N-terminal residues that affect protein stability.

claim: DPP9 cleavage is permissive towards more amino acids in the P1' position (Xaa-Ala/Pro-Zaa), and is only inhibited if the residue after the cleavage site (Zaa) is Pro.
source: In contrast to MetAPs, DPP9 cleavage is permissive towards more amino acids in the P1' position (Xaa-Ala/Pro-Zaa), and is only inhibited if the residue after the cleavage site (Zaa) is Pro (Geiss-Friedlander et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Geiss-Friedlander et al., 2009.

claim: DPP9 may directly produce an N-degron not requiring further modification.
source: Therefore DPP9 may directly produce an N-degron not requiring further modification (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the substrate specificity of DPP9.

claim: DPP9 can cleave substrates with any amino acid in the P2 position (Xaa) apart from Asp or Glu.
source: Additionally, DPP9 can cleave substrates with any amino acid in the P2 position (Xaa) apart from Asp or Glu, greatly increasing the number of potential substrates, including proteins undergoing progressive processing (Geiss-Friedlander et al., 2009; Connolly et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Geiss-Friedlander et al., 2009 and Connolly et al., 2008.

claim: MetAPs function largely in a co-translational manner.
source: Whereas MetAPs function largely in a co-translational manner, our data strongly suggest that DPP9 acts in a post-translational manner.
evidence: This is established knowledge about MetAPs.

claim: DPP9 acts in a post-translational manner.
source: Whereas MetAPs function largely in a co-translational manner, our data strongly suggest that DPP9 acts in a post-translational manner.
evidence: Inferred from data showing DPP9 cleaves mature Syk protein.

claim: FLNA may serve as an interaction platform linking DPP9 and Syk.
source: Additionally, we found that although DPP9 interacts directly with Syk, in cells this interaction requires FLNA, suggesting that FLNA may serve as an interaction platform linking DPP9 and Syk (Figure 8C).
evidence: Inferred from data showing FLNA silencing reduces DPP9-Syk interaction.

claim: FLNA may support Syk processing by increasing the local concentration of Syk and DPP9, stabilizing the complex formation or by optimizing the orientation of DPP9 and Syk for efficient cleavage.
source: Consequently, FLNA may support Syk processing e.g. by increasing the local concentration of Syk and DPP9, stabilizing the complex formation or by optimizing the orientation of DPP9 and Syk for efficient cleavage.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the role of FLNA as a scaffold protein.

claim: The function of FLNA may parallel that of F-box proteins in the ubiquitin ligase SCF complexes, which bind to substrates and thus support their ubiquitination by ubiquitin conjugating enzymes.
source: In this sense, the function of FLNA may parallel that of F-box proteins in the ubiquitin ligase SCF complexes, which bind to substrates and thus support their ubiquitination by ubiquitin conjugating enzymes (Edward and Kipreos, 2000).
evidence: This is a proposed analogy supported by citation to Edward and Kipreos, 2000.

claim: FLNA may act as a general recruitment factor targeting DPP9 to additional potential substrates for cleavage.
source: Since FLNA interacts with multiple proteins, it is tempting to speculate that it acts as a general recruitment factor targeting DPP9 to additional potential substrates for cleavage.
evidence: This is speculation based on the known properties of FLNA.

claim: Depending on the substrate and the exposed residue in the neo N-terminus, DPP9 may cooperate with Cbl or other E3 ligases that then ubiquitinate the substrate resulting in proteasomal degradation.
source: We suggest that depending on the substrate and the exposed residue in the neo N-terminus, DPP9 may cooperate with Cbl or other E3 ligases that then ubiquitinate the substrate resulting in proteasomal degradation.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on experimental data.

claim: FLNA was identified in 12 of 142 processed clones in the yeast two-hybrid screen.
source: FLNA was one of the most promising candidates, which was identified in 12 of 142 processed clones.
evidence: This is data from the yeast two-hybrid screen.

claim: The binding surface between DPP9 and FLNA was mapped to residues 748–907 of FLNA, corresponding to FLNA repeats 5–7.
source: The binding surface was mapped to residues 748–907 of FLNA, corresponding to FLNA repeats 5–7.
evidence: This is data from the yeast two-hybrid screen.

claim: The interaction between FLNA and Syk was first identified in platelets.
source: The interaction between FLNA and Syk was identified in platelets, where loss of FLNA resulted in reduced signalling and mislocalization of Syk (Falet et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Falet et al., 2010.

claim: Loss of FLNA in platelets resulted in reduced signalling and mislocalization of Syk.
source: The interaction between FLNA and Syk was identified in platelets, where loss of FLNA resulted in reduced signalling and mislocalization of Syk (Falet et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Falet et al., 2010.

claim: The association between FLNA and Syk is conserved in HeLa cells.
source: By PLA we show that the association between FLNA and Syk, which was first identified in platelets, is conserved in HeLa cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by proximity ligation assay shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Amino acids 1–7 of Syk are not resolved in any determined structure of Syk.
source: Of note, amino acids 1–7 are not resolved in any determined structure of Syk, suggesting that this region is flexible and thus accessible for interactions.
evidence: This is based on published structures cited as Grädler et al., 2013 and Fütterer et al., 1998.

claim: The N-terminal region (amino acids 1-7) of Syk is flexible and accessible for interactions.
source: Of note, amino acids 1–7 are not resolved in any determined structure of Syk, suggesting that this region is flexible and thus accessible for interactions.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of structural resolution in published structures.

claim: Syk is best characterized as an essential component in B cell receptor (BCR) mediated signalling.
source: Although it is also expressed in non-haematopoietic cells, Syk is best characterized as an essential component in B cell receptor (BCR) mediated signalling.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Syk is activated upon BCR engagement, and consequently initiates a cascade of events by phosphorylating its downstream effectors.
source: Syk is activated upon BCR engagement, and consequently initiates a cascade of events by phosphorylating its downstream effectors (Mócsai et al., 2010; Geahlen, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mócsai et al., 2010 and Geahlen, 2009.

claim: Syk signalling can be terminated by degradation, requiring the ubiquitin E3 ligase Cbl.
source: Syk signalling can be terminated by degradation, requiring the ubiquitin E3 ligase Cbl.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in the manuscript.

claim: DPP9 forms a complex with FLNA and Syk.
source: Here we show that DPP9 forms a complex with FLNA and Syk.
evidence: Supported by proximity ligation assays and co-immunoprecipitation experiments.

claim: In the DPP9-FLNA-Syk complex, FLNA acts as a recruiting factor linking DPP9 to Syk.
source: In this complex FLNA acts as a recruiting factor linking DPP9 to Syk, resulting in cleavage of the Syk N-terminus by DPP9, thus affecting Syk stability and Syk dependent signal transduction.
evidence: Inferred from data showing FLNA is required for DPP9-Syk interaction in cells.

claim: Cleavage of the Syk N-terminus by DPP9 affects Syk stability and Syk dependent signal transduction.
source: In this complex FLNA acts as a recruiting factor linking DPP9 to Syk, resulting in cleavage of the Syk N-terminus by DPP9, thus affecting Syk stability and Syk dependent signal transduction.
evidence: Supported by cycloheximide chase experiments and signaling assays.
